title: Fixed-Price Contract (Software)
seoDescription: A fixed-price software contract sets one price for an agreed scope. When it protects you, when time-and-materials is better, and clauses to check.
summary: A fixed-price software contract sets one price for an agreed scope of work, so the vendor carries the risk of overruns within that scope. It suits well-defined projects; for evolving requirements, time-and-materials or phased fixed prices usually give better results.

dataPoints.label: Suits
dataPoints.value: Clear scope, stable requirements, short to medium projects

dataPoints.label: Alternative
dataPoints.value: Time-and-materials: pay for hours used, with regular reviews

dataPoints.label: Common middle ground
dataPoints.value: Paid discovery, then fixed price per phase

dataPoints.label: Watch for
dataPoints.value: Vague scope, expensive change requests, quality cut to protect margin

body:
## Protect yourself in either model

- A written scope with acceptance criteria.
- Milestones tied to working, tested features.
- A change-request process with rates agreed upfront.
- Code ownership and handover clauses.

See [fixed price vs time and materials](/blog/fixed-price-vs-time-and-materials-which-software-contract-protects-you) and [how to write a software brief that gets accurate quotes](/blog/how-to-write-a-software-brief-that-gets-accurate-quotes).

faqs.a: No. Vendors add buffers for risk, and change requests can add up. It is more predictable, not necessarily cheaper.
Yes, if agreed. Many projects start fixed-price for a defined phase and move to time-and-materials for later improvements.
